Bio:
Anya V. Egorova (she/her/hers) is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at the University of Alabama. Her research interest lies in data mining, natural language processing, and data-driven approaches for understanding human and organizational behavior. Her projects focus on social, business, political, and educational data using computational and machine learning methods to uncover hidden patterns, generate actionable insights, and improve understanding of human behavior. She is a recipient of the 2021 Best Paper Award (ACM SIGKDD) for “Using Word Embedding Networks to Identify and Explain Unfair Bias in Algorithms,” and the 2021 Best Paper Award at Data for Social Good 2021 in the Track: Health Disparities and COVID-19: Equity and Disparities. Anya holds a Ph.D. and M.S. in Computer Science from Carnegie Mellon University and a B.S. in Computer Science from Moscow State University.

Abstract:
This paper studies the use of the optimal power flow (OPF) problem as the basis for optimal dispatch of power in a hybrid wind-diesel-micro-hydro-storage isolated power system. The problem formulation allows the simultaneous consideration of economic, system reliability, environmental, and dynamic dispatch constraints. A mixed integer-linear formulation of the OPF problem is proposed in order to enable the direct utilization of the conventional OPF solution methods. The proposed mixed-integer-linear OPF is applied to a case study based on the existing isolated power system of the Greek island of Tilos. The results of an extensive parametric analysis are presented, and a discussion of some of the key implications of the study on the planning and operation of future isolated power systems is given.
Abstract:
This paper presents an iterative approach to the design of an integrated system architecture for energy management systems (EMS) and distribution system operation. The proposed architecture is based on the integration of three components: a centralized EMS, a distributed EMS, and the existing distribution network control systems. Two design scenarios are considered. In the first scenario, it is assumed that only a subset of the control entities and devices of the existing system are compatible with the new EMS architecture. In the second scenario, which is considered the ideal case, all existing control entities and devices are compatible with the EMS architecture. The proposed architecture is applied to a modified IEEE 13-bus test system. The performance of the EMS is illustrated through case studies for the day-ahead optimal power flow and the real-time EMS control problems.

Abstract:
The effect of various materials on a human mandible fracture repair was evaluated. A series of tests were carried out on mandibularcantilever beam specimens cut from fresh and frozen cadaver heads. Human mandible specimens were reinforced by different composites, including carbon fiberreinforced composites and fiberglass-reinforced composites. The reinforcement methods used were adhesive bonding and embedding, and all the test specimenswere loaded to fracture in an Instron testing machine. Load-deflection graphs were recorded, from which the bending moment that causes fracture in the different specimen types was obtained and the failure type and load-bearing mechanism were investigated. The test results showed that a composite reinforcement could effectively increase the strength and stiffness of a human mandible fracture. Fiberglass-reinforced composites were the best reinforcing material for human mandibles.

Objectives: (i) To determine the clinical and treatment outcomes following SAMMPRIS protocol in real life; (ii) To evaluate the compliance with the SAMMPRIS guidelines and the impact on clinical outcome; (iii) To identify the factors which have a predictive impact on the patient's clinical outcome. Methods: 73 consecutive patients who underwent angiographic demonstration of ICAD from February 2004 to November 2009 were retrospectively analyzed. The clinical and angiographic characteristics of these patients were recorded in a database. The clinical and angiographic status of the patients were followed prospectively for 6 months after AMM intervention. Results: Overall, 26 patients underwent surgery with a morbidity rate of 23% and mortality rate of 7.7%. All of the patients who had ischemic stroke had undergone angioplasty or surgery. Of the 47 patients who received AMM (9 underwent carotid endarterectomy after AMM treatment had failed), 43 patients showed stable neurologic deficits while 2 patients experienced stroke or hemorrhage within 6 months of AMM therapy. Conclusions: The overall complication rate for surgery was significantly higher than that for AMM therapy. There is a high level of compliance with the SAMMPRIS recommendation of AMM with 25% of patients opting for surgery. There was a low frequency of new neurological events at 6 months with AMM therapy. Patients should be informed about the benefit/risk balance of surgical and AMM treatment prior to deciding on any particular treatment method.
